title: The diamond rings
body: A high-ranking British officer visits Pratibandapuram. He loves hunting tigers and loves even more being photographed with the tigers he has shot. The Maharaja, who has vowed to kill a hundred tigers himself, refuses him permission and offers a boar hunt, a mouse hunt or even a mosquito hunt instead. The officer's secretary then suggests that the Maharaja may do the actual killing, as long as the officer gets a photograph of himself holding the gun and standing over the carcass. The Maharaja refuses this too. Now he is in danger of losing his kingdom. After talking it over with the dewan, he wires a famous British firm of jewellers in Calcutta for samples of expensive diamond rings. About fifty rings arrive, and the Maharaja sends all of them to the officer's wife, expecting her to keep one or two and return the rest. She promptly writes back to thank him for his gifts. Two days later a bill for three lakh of rupees arrives, and the Maharaja is happy that, though he has lost the money, he has kept his kingdom.

title: The hundredth tiger falls
body: The dewan secretly brings an old tiger from the People's Park in Madras and, at midnight, he and his aged wife drive it to the forest where the Maharaja is hunting. The next day the tiger wanders up to the Maharaja and stands before him as if humbly waiting for orders. The Maharaja takes careful aim, the tiger falls in a heap, and the overjoyed king declares that his vow is fulfilled. He orders the tiger to be carried to the capital in a grand procession and drives away. When the hunters look closely, they find the tiger alive and rolling its eyes in bafflement: the bullet had missed, and the animal had only fainted from the shock of it whizzing past. They agree that the Maharaja must never know he missed. One of them shoots the tiger from a foot away and kills it. The dead tiger is then taken in procession through the town, buried, and a tomb is raised over it.
